title: The American Soldier and Relative Deprivation
text:
During World War II, the US Army created a Research Branch staffed by social scientists, led by sociologist Samuel Stouffer. They surveyed hundreds of thousands of American soldiers about their attitudes, morale and experiences. After the war, Stouffer and his colleagues published the results in a series of volumes called The American Soldier.

One finding puzzled them. In the Army Air Forces, promotion was fast and common. In the Military Police, it was slow and rare. Yet Air Forces men were more critical of the promotion system and more likely to say a capable soldier had a poor chance of advancing, while Military Police men were more satisfied with their chances.

The researchers explained this by what they called relative deprivation. People judged their situation not by an absolute standard but by comparing themselves with others around them. A soldier in the Air Forces who had not been promoted saw many of his peers moving up and felt left behind. A military policeman who had not been promoted saw that most of his peers had not been either. Similar comparisons appeared elsewhere in the surveys, for example in how married and single men felt about being drafted.
lesson: Satisfaction depends on comparison with nearby peers. When rewarding a team, consider how people will see their outcome next to their colleagues', not only its size.
people: Samuel Stouffer, Edward Suchman, Leland DeVinney, Shirley Star, Robin Williams
source: Stouffer, S. A., Suchman, E. A., DeVinney, L. C., Star, S. A., and Williams, R. M. (1949). The American Soldier: Adjustment During Army Life. Princeton University Press.
